blocks.text: You stub your toe on a chair leg. First comes a sharp, exactly located stab, and a second or so later a deep, throbbing ache that spreads and lingers. Two different pain sensations from one injury, arriving at different times, tell us that two different kinds of nerve fibre carry them.

blocks.markdown:
**Nociception** is the neural detection of tissue-damaging stimuli. **Nociceptors** are free nerve endings that respond to intense mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli, and are sensitised by inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P). Their axons are of two types.

- **A-delta fibres**: thinly **myelinated**, about 2-5 micrometres in diameter, conducting at roughly 5-30 m/s. They signal **fast, sharp, well-localised 'first' pain**.
- **C fibres**: **unmyelinated**, thinner, conducting at about 0.5-2 m/s. They signal **slow, dull, burning or aching, poorly localised 'second' pain**.

Both types have their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion and synapse in the **dorsal horn** (laminae I, II and V), releasing glutamate and the neuropeptide **substance P**. Second-order neurones cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the **anterolateral (spinothalamic) system** to the thalamus (VPL nucleus) and then the somatosensory cortex for localisation and quality (the **neospinothalamic** pathway, largely from A-delta fibres), while a slower, more diffuse **paleospinothalamic** route to the reticular formation, medial thalamus and limbic structures (anterior cingulate, insula) carries the **emotional and unpleasant** dimension.

rows: Paleospinothalamic: reticular formation, medial thalamus, limbic cortex

blocks.title: The delay between first and second pain
blocks.prompt: A noxious stimulus is applied to the hand, 0.9 m from the brain along the pathway. A-delta fibres conduct at 18 m/s and C fibres at 0.9 m/s. How much later does second pain arrive?
blocks.answer: Second pain arrives about 0.95 s (950 ms) after first pain.

blocks.markdown:
**Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall).** In the dorsal horn, the transmission of nociceptive signals to projection neurones is regulated by an inhibitory interneurone in the **substantia gelatinosa**. **Large-diameter A-beta touch fibres** excite this inhibitory interneurone and so **close the gate**, reducing pain transmission. **Small nociceptive C fibres** inhibit the interneurone and so **open the gate**. This explains why rubbing a bumped shin reduces pain, and is the rationale for transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). Descending pathways also act on the gate.

**Descending modulation.** The **periaqueductal grey (PAG)** of the midbrain is activated by the cortex, hypothalamus and by opioids. It projects to the **rostral ventromedial medulla (nucleus raphe magnus)**, which sends serotonergic (and with the locus coeruleus, noradrenergic) fibres down the dorsolateral funiculus to the dorsal horn. These activate **enkephalin-containing interneurones**, which inhibit presynaptic release of substance P and hyperpolarise projection neurones. Endogenous opioids (enkephalins, endorphins, dynorphins) act on opioid receptors, and morphine acts mainly on the **mu receptor** at these sites in the PAG, medulla and dorsal horn.

blocks.title: Why rubbing helps
blocks.prompt: Explain, using the gate control theory, why rubbing the skin near a painful area relieves the pain.

steps.text: Rubbing activates large myelinated A-beta mechanoreceptor afferents.
These excite inhibitory interneurones in the substantia gelatinosa.
The interneurones inhibit the projection neurones receiving C and A-delta nociceptive input, closing the gate.

blocks.answer: A-beta activity closes the gate on pain transmission in the dorsal horn, so less nociceptive signal is relayed to the thalamus.

blocks.markdown: **Referred pain** is pain perceived in a part of the body distant from the source. **Mechanism (convergence-projection):** visceral nociceptive afferents and somatic afferents from a particular skin area enter the cord at the same segments and converge on the same second-order dorsal horn neurones. Since the brain is far more used to signals from skin than from viscera, it interprets the visceral signal as arising from the skin area supplied by the same segment. Examples: **myocardial ischaemia** is felt in the **left arm and jaw** and chest (T1-T4); **diaphragmatic irritation** (for example by blood or inflamed gallbladder) is felt at the **shoulder tip** because the diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) and the skin of the shoulder tip by C3-C5 dermatomes; early **appendicitis** is felt around the **umbilicus** (T10) before the pain moves to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum is irritated.

blocks.title: Pain is not only afferent
blocks.text: The pain experienced is the net result of nociceptive input and descending modulation. The same stimulus can be felt as more or less painful depending on attention, emotion and opioid-mediated inhibition.

points: A-delta fibres carry fast, sharp, well-localised pain; C fibres carry slow, dull, burning pain; both relay in the dorsal horn and ascend in the spinothalamic system.
Gate control theory: large A-beta fibres close the gate through inhibitory interneurones in the substantia gelatinosa; C fibres open it.
Descending control runs from the PAG through the rostral ventromedial medulla to the dorsal horn, using serotonin, noradrenaline and enkephalins; opioids act at mu receptors.
Referred pain arises because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same dorsal horn neurones.

questions.stem: Which fibre type transmits fast, sharp, well-localised pain?

options.text: A-beta fibres
A-delta fibres
C fibres
A-alpha fibres

distractorRationale.b: Correct: thinly myelinated A-delta fibres signal first pain.
distractorRationale.c: C fibres signal slow, dull pain.
distractorRationale.d: A-alpha fibres carry proprioception and motor signals.

questions.explanation: Thinly myelinated A-delta fibres conduct relatively rapidly and give the sharp, well-localised first pain. C fibres give the delayed dull ache.

questions.stem: A patient describes a deep, burning, poorly localised ache that persists after a burn. Which fibres mainly mediate this pain?

options.text: Unmyelinated C fibres
Myelinated A-beta fibres
A-alpha fibres
Preganglionic sympathetic fibres

distractorRationale.b: A-beta fibres carry touch and would not produce burning pain.
distractorRationale.c: A-alpha fibres are large proprioceptive and motor fibres.

questions.explanation: A slow, dull, burning, poorly localised ache is second pain, carried by unmyelinated C fibres.

questions.stem: A pinprick is applied to the foot, which is 1.2 m from the brain along the pathway. A-delta fibres conduct at 15 m/s and C fibres at 1.0 m/s. By how many milliseconds does the arrival of C-fibre signals lag that of A-delta signals?
questions.explanation: A-delta time = 1.2/15 = 0.08 s = 80 ms. C time = 1.2/1.0 = 1.2 s = 1200 ms. The lag is 1200 - 80 = 1120 ms, which is why the dull second pain is felt more than a second after the sharp first pain.

questions.stem: According to gate control theory, activity in which fibres closes the gate in the dorsal horn?

options.text: Large-diameter A-beta touch fibres, via inhibitory interneurones
Small unmyelinated C fibres
Sympathetic postganglionic fibres
Motor axons in the ventral root

questions.correctOptionText: Large-diameter A-beta touch fibres, via inhibitory interneurones

distractorRationale.c: Sympathetic fibres are not part of the gate.

questions.explanation: A-beta fibre activity excites inhibitory interneurones in the substantia gelatinosa, reducing nociceptive transmission. This is the basis of rubbing a painful area or applying TENS.

questions.stem: Which pathway forms the main descending route for endogenous pain modulation?

options.text: Periaqueductal grey, rostral ventromedial medulla, then the dorsal horn
Cerebellum, red nucleus, then the ventral horn
Hippocampus, fornix, then the mammillary bodies
Basal ganglia, thalamus, then motor cortex

questions.correctOptionText: Periaqueductal grey, rostral ventromedial medulla, then the dorsal horn

distractorRationale.c: This is the memory circuit of Papez.

questions.explanation: The PAG activates the rostral ventromedial medulla (nucleus raphe magnus), which projects to the dorsal horn and inhibits nociceptive transmission through serotonin and enkephalin interneurones.

questions.stem: True or false: morphine produces analgesia mainly by acting on mu opioid receptors in the periaqueductal grey, medulla and dorsal horn. (Pharmacology teaching example.)

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Morphine mimics endogenous opioids at mu receptors, activating the descending PAG-medullary pathway and inhibiting dorsal horn transmission. Receptors in these regions account for much of its analgesic effect.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a crushing central chest pain radiating down the left arm and into the jaw. Which mechanism best explains the arm and jaw pain?

options.text: Cardiac visceral afferents converge with somatic afferents of the same cord segments on shared dorsal horn neurones
Direct spread of ischaemia to the arm muscles
Vagal fibres supply the arm skin
The arm has its own heart-related nociceptors

questions.correctOptionText: Cardiac visceral afferents converge with somatic afferents of the same cord segments on shared dorsal horn neurones

distractorRationale.b: Ischaemia is in the myocardium, not the arm muscles.
distractorRationale.c: The vagus does not supply arm skin.
distractorRationale.d: There are no heart-specific nociceptors in the arm.

questions.explanation: Cardiac nociceptive afferents enter the upper thoracic cord and converge on the same neurones that receive input from the arm. The brain interprets the signal as arising from the skin, so the pain is referred to the arm and jaw.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old has pain first felt around the umbilicus that, after hours, localises to the right iliac fossa. Which explanation correctly accounts for the shift?

options.text: Early pain arises from visceral afferents (T10, referred to the umbilicus); later pain arises from irritation of the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic localisation
The appendix moves to the right iliac fossa
The vagus nerve first signals pain and then the phrenic nerve takes over
C fibres are replaced by A-beta fibres

questions.correctOptionText: Early pain arises from visceral afferents (T10, referred to the umbilicus); later pain arises from irritation of the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic localisation

distractorRationale.c: The phrenic nerve is not involved.

questions.explanation: Visceral pain from the appendix is poorly localised and referred to the T10 dermatome at the umbilicus. When the inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, somatic afferents give sharp, well-localised pain in the right iliac fossa.

questions.stem: Explain the mechanism of referred pain, using a patient with an inflamed gallbladder who feels pain at the tip of the right shoulder.
markingGuide: Visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same second-order dorsal horn neurones
Brain interprets visceral input as coming from the somatic area of the same segment
Diaphragmatic irritation by the inflamed gallbladder activates phrenic afferents (C3-C5)
The shoulder tip skin is supplied by C3-C5, so pain is felt there
Pain is perceived at a site distant from the source
questions.explanation: The central part of the diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), and the shoulder tip skin by the same segments. Convergence of these inputs on shared dorsal horn neurones makes the brain locate the pain at the shoulder.

questions.stem: Describe how endogenous descending pathways reduce pain transmission in the dorsal horn and how opioid drugs enhance this.
markingGuide: PAG is activated by cortex, hypothalamus and opioids
PAG projects to the rostral ventromedial medulla (nucleus raphe magnus)
Descending serotonergic and noradrenergic fibres reach the dorsal horn
Enkephalin interneurones inhibit substance P release and hyperpolarise projection neurones
Opioids such as morphine act on mu receptors in the PAG, medulla and dorsal horn, mimicking endogenous opioids
questions.explanation: The descending system lets the brain gate nociceptive input at its first synapse. Opioids act at the same sites and receptors as endogenous opioid peptides, strengthening this inhibition.
